rw: Reacting angrily without thinking shows poor self-regulation. When plans change, low emotional intelligence leads to outbursts that harm relationships and judgment.

ww.Admitting your own mistakes openly to al: Admitting your own mistakes openly shows self-awareness and accountability, which are signs of high emotional intelligence. It is a healthy habit, not a weakness.
ww.Listening closely to other people's conc: Listening closely to other people's concerns shows empathy and social awareness. Those are signs of high emotional intelligence, not low.
ww.Staying calm and steady under pressure a: Staying calm and steady under pressure is a sign of strong self-regulation. It helps people think clearly and keeps teams stable, so it is high emotional intelligence.

rw: A prototype is an early sample of a product used for testing ideas. It lets an entrepreneur find flaws and gather feedback before paying for full production.

ww.A permanent store location for the busin: A permanent store location is a place of business. A prototype is a test model of a product, not a place where goods are sold.
ww.A final report that is sent to investors: A final report to investors is a document. A prototype is a physical or working model, and it comes before a final product.
ww.A legal document that proves ownership o: Proof of ownership is shown by legal papers. A prototype is a test version of a product, not a legal record.

rw: Crowdfunding raises small amounts of money from many people, usually through an online platform. Backers may get rewards, products or a share in the business.

ww.Receiving a tax refund from the governme: A tax refund is money returned by the government. It is not raised from many supporters to fund a new project.
ww.Borrowing one large sum from a single ba: Borrowing one large sum from a single bank is a bank loan. Crowdfunding gathers small amounts from many people instead.
ww.Selling the whole business to a single b: Selling the whole business is an exit. Crowdfunding raises money while the founder keeps running the project.

rw: A small pilot batch lets the entrepreneur test demand and collect feedback with little money at risk. They can adjust before spending more.

ww.Skip testing and rely on a hunch about w: Skipping testing and relying on a hunch invites costly mistakes. With limited cash, the entrepreneur needs evidence that customers want the product.
ww.Borrow heavily to open several new store: Borrowing heavily to open several stores is very risky with limited cash. If the product fails, the debts remain.
ww.Produce a very large inventory before te: Making a very large inventory before testing demand ties up money in goods that may not sell. It is the opposite of a low-risk test.

rw: A target market is the specific group of customers a business aims to serve. Knowing it helps choose products, prices and advertising.

ww.The competitors that the business faces: Competitors are rival businesses. A target market is the group of customers a business tries to serve.
ww.The employees who work for the company i: Employees are staff who work for the company. They are not the customers the business is trying to reach.
ww.Every single person in the world who mig: Trying to reach every person in the world is not a target market. A target market is a defined group, since no product suits everyone.

rw: Risk tolerance describes how much uncertainty and possible loss an entrepreneur will accept. It shapes choices such as borrowing, investing and trying new ideas.

ww.How many employees they are able to supe: The number of employees a person can supervise is their span of control. Risk tolerance is about how much uncertainty and loss a person will accept.
ww.How many customers the business has serv: The number of customers served is a measure of sales success. Risk tolerance describes an attitude to risk, not performance.
ww.How much profit the business made last y: Last year's profit is a result. Risk tolerance describes how willing the entrepreneur is to face uncertainty.

rw: A balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time. It is a snapshot of the firm's financial position.

ww.Cash flow report: A cash flow report tracks money moving in and out over a period. It does not show assets, liabilities and equity on one date.
ww.Budget plan: A budget plan forecasts income and spending. It is a plan, not a report of what a company owns and owes.
ww.Income report: An income report covers revenue and expenses over a period. It does not show what the company owns and owes at one moment.

rw: Owner's equity equals assets minus liabilities. $150,000 minus $90,000 is $60,000, which is the owners' share of the business.

ww.$240,000: $240,000 adds assets and liabilities together. Equity subtracts liabilities from assets, so it must be smaller than assets.
ww.$150,000: $150,000 is the total assets. Equity is what remains after paying the $90,000 of liabilities.
ww.$90,000: $90,000 is the liabilities. Equity is assets minus liabilities, which is $60,000.

rw: Gross profit is sales revenue minus the cost of goods sold. It shows how much is left from sales to pay operating costs.

ww.Total assets minus all the liabilities: Assets minus liabilities gives owner's equity, which is found on the balance sheet. Gross profit is a measure of sales performance.
ww.Cash on hand at the end of each month: Cash on hand is a balance sheet figure. Gross profit is calculated from sales and the cost of goods sold.
ww.Sales revenue minus all expenses and tax: Revenue minus all expenses and taxes is net income. Gross profit subtracts only the direct cost of goods sold.

rw: Net income before taxes is sales minus the cost of goods and operating expenses. $50,000 less $30,000 less $12,000 is $8,000.

ww.$20,000: $20,000 is the gross profit, sales less cost of goods. Operating expenses of $12,000 must still be subtracted to reach $8,000.
ww.$32,000: $32,000 does not follow from the figures. Net income before taxes is $50,000 minus $30,000 minus $12,000, or $8,000.
ww.$92,000: $92,000 adds all the numbers together. Income is found by subtracting costs from sales, which gives $8,000.

rw: Liquidity is how easily an asset can be turned into cash. Cash is the most liquid asset, while property is much harder to sell fast.

ww.How much profit a business earns after c: Profit after costs is net income. Liquidity is about how quickly assets can become cash.
ww.How much debt a business owes to lenders: Debt owed to lenders is a liability. It does not measure how easily assets turn into cash.
ww.How long a business has existed up to no: How long a business has existed is its age. It has no bearing on liquidity.

rw: An employee handbook explains company policies, rules and expectations. It tells staff about conduct, benefits and procedures in one place.

ww.To track the daily sales of the business: Daily sales tracking is done through sales reports. An employee handbook is for staff, not owners.
ww.To list each of the customer's recent pu: Customer purchases belong in sales or customer records. They are unrelated to a staff guide.
ww.To set the price of the company's stock: The price of stock is set by the market. A handbook does not decide it.

rw: Onboarding helps new employees learn the job and the company. Good onboarding helps them settle in faster and stay longer.

ww.The process of ending an employee's cont: Ending a contract is called termination. Onboarding is the opposite, welcoming and training a new hire.
ww.The process of paying overtime to employ: Paying overtime is part of payroll. Onboarding is about training new employees.
ww.The process of advertising an open job p: Advertising an open position is recruitment. Onboarding comes after the person is hired.

rw: Recognizing the work and discussing development or promotion rewards effort. It keeps the employee motivated and builds loyalty.

ww.Ignore the performance to avoid jealousy: Ignoring strong performance can discourage the employee. Managers should recognize good work, not hide it.
ww.Give the employee more work with no reco: Giving more work with no recognition or pay discussion feels unfair. It could cause the employee to leave.
ww.Reduce the employee's pay to match that: Cutting pay to match peers punishes good work. It would likely cause the employee to resign.

rw: A wage is paid per hour worked, while a salary is a fixed amount per year. Wage earners are often paid for the exact hours they work.

ww.A wage is a fixed amount per year; a sal: This reverses the two terms. A wage is hourly, and a salary is fixed per year.
ww.Wages are tips given by customers; salar: Tips and bonuses are extra forms of pay. Wages and salaries are the base pay for work.
ww.There is no difference between the two t: The terms differ in how pay is calculated. Wages depend on hours and salaries are fixed.

rw: Exit interviews help companies learn why employees leave and how to improve. The answers can reveal problems with pay, management or culture.

ww.To reduce the paychecks of staff who are: Exit interviews do not cut pay. They gather feedback from people who are leaving.
ww.To convince employees to quit sooner tha: Companies do not hold exit interviews to push staff out. The employee has already decided to go.
ww.To hire the same employee back at once f: Rehiring someone is not the goal. The interview aims to learn from the experience.

rw: A password manager stores and generates strong, unique passwords securely. It lets people use a different strong password for each account without memorizing them.

ww.Deleting old accounts automatically each: It does not delete accounts automatically. Its job is to hold passwords, not to remove accounts.
ww.Replacing the need for any other kind of: It does not replace other security. Firms still need protections such as firewalls and updates.
ww.Sharing passwords with all coworkers ope: Sharing passwords openly weakens security. A password manager protects them, and sharing should be limited and controlled.

rw: Encryption scrambles data so only authorized people with the key can read it. Even if it is stolen, it stays unreadable.

ww.Makes it larger so that it is easier to: Encryption does not make data bigger so it is easier to find. It changes the data into a coded form.
ww.Copies it to a public site for anyone to: Copying data to a public site would expose it. Encryption protects it.
ww.Deletes it permanently from the disk of: Deleting data permanently is erasure. Encryption keeps the data but makes it unreadable without a key.

rw: Full-disk encryption scrambles everything stored on the laptop. A thief cannot read the customer records without the key, so harm is limited.

ww.A faster internet link: A faster internet link would not protect stored records. The data would still be readable if the laptop was stolen.
ww.A longer warranty plan: A longer warranty covers repairs. It does nothing to protect the data on a stolen laptop.
ww.A brightly colored bag: A bag may be eye-catching, but it does not protect data. Encryption is the control that matters.

rw: Customer comments about why they like a product are descriptive and based on opinion. That makes them qualitative data.

ww.The total revenue for the quarter in dol: Revenue in dollars is numerical data, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data describes opinions or qualities.
ww.The number of units sold last month by e: Units sold is a count, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data is descriptive.
ww.The average price of items sold in the s: An average price is a number, so it is quantitative. Qualitative data is not measured in numbers.

rw: Cloud storage lets a small business reach its files from many devices without owning servers. That saves money and gives flexibility.

ww.Internet access is no longer needed for: Cloud storage depends on the internet. Access needs a connection, so it does not remove the need for it.
ww.All backups of the files become unnecess: Backups are still important. Cloud services can fail, so firms still need copies.
ww.Files can never be lost or hacked in any: Cloud files can be lost or hacked. No service guarantees against loss or attack.

rw: Branding creates a recognizable identity that sets a business apart. A strong brand helps customers remember and trust the business.

ww.Increase the number of competitors in th: Branding does not increase competitors. It helps a business stand out from them.
ww.Lower the cost of the raw materials that: Branding does not lower material costs. It shapes how customers see the firm.
ww.Remove the need for any advertising at a: Branding supports advertising and does not replace it. Firms still need to promote their products.

rw: Penetration pricing sets a low price to attract customers fast in a new market. The low price wins market share, and the firm may raise it later.

ww.Price skimming strategy: Price skimming starts high and lowers over time. It is the opposite of a low price used to enter a market quickly.
ww.Prestige pricing: Prestige pricing sets a high price to suggest quality. It does not aim to attract customers with low prices.
ww.Cost-plus pricing: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to costs. It is not designed to win a new market quickly.

rw: Price skimming sets a high price at first and lowers it over time. It earns more from early buyers before bringing in price-conscious customers.

ww.Loss leader: A loss leader is a product sold below cost to bring in customers. It is not a high starting price that falls over time.
ww.Bundle pricing: Bundle pricing sells items together at one price. It does not start high and drop later.
ww.Penetration: Penetration pricing starts low to win a market. It is the opposite of skimming.

rw: Loss leader pricing sells a product below cost to bring shoppers in. The store hopes they buy other items at normal prices.

ww.Price skimming strategy: Price skimming starts high on a new product. Selling milk below cost to draw shoppers is the opposite.
ww.Cost-plus pricing: Cost-plus pricing adds a markup to cost. A below-cost price does not follow that method.
ww.Prestige pricing: Prestige pricing sets a high price to signal quality. Selling below cost is not a prestige approach.

rw: A distribution channel is the path a product takes from the producer to the final customer. It may include wholesalers and retailers.

ww.A group of employees who work together i: A group of employees working together is a team. A distribution channel is the route products take.
ww.A law that sets rules about product pric: A law on pricing is a regulation. A distribution channel is about moving goods.
ww.A television network that is used for ad: A TV network is an advertising medium. A distribution channel moves products, not messages.

rw: A purchase order formally requests goods or services from a supplier. It sets out quantities, prices and delivery terms.

ww.To bill a customer for goods that were r: Billing a customer is the role of an invoice. A purchase order is a buyer's request to a supplier.
ww.To pay an employee for the hours worked: Paying an employee is done through payroll. A purchase order is for buying goods or services.
ww.To record the goods that have arrived at: Recording goods that have arrived is the job of a receiving report. A purchase order is made before they arrive.

rw: Resolving the difference before paying prevents overpaying. The buyer should pay for the 90 units that arrived and ask for a corrected invoice.

ww.Pay the full invoice amount without chec: Paying the full invoice means paying for 10 units that never arrived. It wastes money.
ww.Refuse to ever do business with the supp: Refusing to deal with the supplier again is an overreaction. A one-time error can be fixed by talking to them.
ww.Throw away the invoice and forget about: Throwing away the invoice leaves the account unresolved. The supplier could chase payment later.

rw: Preventive maintenance reduces breakdowns and unplanned downtime. Regular servicing finds small faults before they become costly failures.

ww.It guarantees equipment will never be re: Preventive maintenance does not stop replacement forever. All equipment wears out eventually.
ww.It removes the need for equipment operat: Operators are still needed. Maintenance keeps equipment working but does not replace people.
ww.It increases accidents on the shop floor: Maintenance reduces accidents because equipment is in better condition. It does not increase them.

rw: Production capacity is the maximum amount a business can produce in a period. It sets the limit on how much it can sell without expanding.

ww.The number of customers served in a day: Customers served per day measure demand or traffic. Capacity is about output.
ww.The minimum price of a product on the sh: A minimum price is a pricing idea. Capacity is about the largest output.
ww.The profit earned per unit sold by the f: Profit per unit is a measure of earnings. Capacity is about quantity produced.

rw: Teamwork is a soft skill, an interpersonal ability. It is useful in almost any job.

ww.Forklift use: Forklift use is a hard skill, a technical ability learned through training. Soft skills are interpersonal.
ww.Software use: Software use is a hard skill that can be taught and measured. Soft skills are personal qualities.
ww.Writing code: Writing code is a technical, hard skill. It differs from interpersonal soft skills.

rw: Professional networking means building relationships that offer advice and chances. Contacts can share job leads, mentoring and support.

ww.Selling products to complete strangers o: Selling to strangers only is a sales approach. Professional networking is about building relationships.
ww.Working alone without any contact with o: Working alone with no contact is the opposite of networking. Networking needs people to connect.
ww.Connecting the computers together in an: Connecting computers is a technical meaning of networking. In a professional context it means connecting with people.

rw: School activities, volunteering and relevant skills show value to employers. They show responsibility and ability, even without work history.

map.A list of every game that I have ever pl: A list of every game that you have ever played at home

ww.Nothing at all, so the page is left blan: A blank page gives employers nothing. A first-time job seeker should list school and volunteer work.
ww.A list of every game that you have ever: A list of games is not relevant to a job. It does not show useful skills.
ww.Invented job titles and made-up skills o: Invented job titles are dishonest. Employers may check, and lying can cost the person the job.

rw: A cover letter introduces you and explains why you fit the job. It shows interest and highlights skills, adding context to your resume.

ww.To request a loan from a local lender or: A loan request goes to a lender. A cover letter is part of a job application.
ww.To list every job that you have ever hel: Listing every job is what a resume does. A cover letter is a short, targeted introduction.
ww.To report your income taxes to the gover: Income taxes are reported on tax forms. A cover letter is for a job application.

rw: A vision statement describes what an organization hopes to become in the future. It inspires staff and gives long-term direction.

ww.A description of the current products an: A description of current products and prices is a product overview. A vision statement looks ahead.
ww.A record of last year's sales figures fo: Last year's sales figures are results. A vision statement describes the future.
ww.A list of employee benefits and perks gi: Employee benefits are part of compensation. A vision statement is not a list of perks.

rw: Strategic planning sets long-term direction. Operational planning covers the daily activities that carry out those plans.

ww.Strategic planning handles daily tasks f: This reverses the two terms. Strategic planning sets long-term goals, and operational planning handles daily work.
ww.Strategic planning ignores goals; operat: Strategic planning does not ignore goals. It sets the long-term direction for the firm.
ww.There is no real difference between the: There is a real difference in time horizon and scope. Strategy is long-term, operations are short-term.

rw: Expansion into a new market means selling to new customers, here in another country. It is a growth decision.

ww.A cost-cutting layoff of staff: A cost-cutting layoff reduces staff. Entering a new country with new products adds to the business, so it is growth.
ww.A shutdown of operations: A shutdown stops operations. The firm is starting in a new country, which is the opposite of closing.
ww.A routine inventory count: An inventory count is a routine check of stock. Entering a new country is a major strategic move.

rw: Benchmarking compares performance with others' best practices. It shows where a business can improve by learning from leaders.

ww.Counting the benches that are in an offi: Counting benches is not a business practice. Benchmarking compares performance with others.
ww.Setting the lowest goals that are possib: Setting the lowest goals does not help improvement. Benchmarking looks at the best.
ww.Ignoring what rivals' results show each: Ignoring rivals is the opposite of benchmarking. It studies other firms' results.

rw: A core competency is a unique strength that gives a business an edge. It is something the firm does especially well that is hard to copy.

ww.A rule imposed by the government on firm: A government rule is a regulation. A core competency is the firm's own strength.
ww.A cost shared among all the firms in a t: A shared industry cost is not a competency. It is something the firm pays.
ww.A weakness the business hopes to hide fr: A weakness is the opposite of a core competency. A core competency is a strength to show off.

rw: A contract is a legally enforceable agreement between two or more parties. If one side breaks it, the other can seek a remedy in court.

ww.A report of a company's earnings for the: A report of future earnings is a forecast. A contract is an agreement.
ww.A list of rules posted on the wall of a: A list of posted rules is a notice. It is not an agreement that binds parties.
ww.A casual promise between friends with no: A casual promise between friends is usually not meant to have legal weight. Contracts are enforceable by law.

rw: Consideration is something of value that each party gives in a contract. It can be money, goods, services or a promise to act.

ww.A polite gesture shown by one side to th: Politeness is not consideration. Consideration is an exchange of value.
ww.The time a party spends thinking about t: Thinking time is not consideration. Consideration is what each side gives or promises.
ww.The fee paid to a court to register the: A court fee is not consideration. Consideration is value exchanged between the parties.

rw: A minor generally lacks full contractual capacity, so can usually cancel most contracts. This protects young people from unfair deals.

ww.A manager: A manager is an adult employee who can be bound by contracts. Age is not an obstacle.
ww.A customer: A customer who is an adult can be bound by a contract. Being a customer does not give a way out.
ww.An adult: An adult has full capacity to make contracts. Adults can generally be held to them.

rw: A breach of contract is a failure to carry out a duty required by the agreement. The other party may seek damages or other remedies.

ww.Asking a lawyer to review the agreement: Asking a lawyer to review an agreement is wise. It is not a breach.
ww.Negotiating the terms with the other sid: Negotiating terms before signing is normal. It is part of forming a contract, not breaking one.
ww.Carrying out every duty on the agreed da: Doing every duty on time is the opposite of a breach. It is full performance of the contract.

rw: Delivering 300 chairs on June 15 instead of 500 by June 1 breaks the contract terms. That is a breach of contract.

ww.A tax law violation: Tax law violation concerns unpaid taxes. The vendor failed to deliver what was promised, which is a contract issue.
ww.A valid change to terms: A valid change to terms needs both sides to agree. The vendor simply delivered less and late.
ww.A trademark dispute: A trademark dispute concerns brand names. The problem here is about delivery, not names.

rw: The UCC makes the laws for sales of goods more consistent among states. That helps businesses trade across state lines.

ww.To set the tax rate on every sale of goo: The UCC does not set sales tax. Tax rates are set by governments.
ww.To control the hiring and firing of work: The UCC does not control hiring and firing. It is about commercial deals such as sales of goods.
ww.To replace the need for written contract: The UCC does not remove the need for written contracts. In some cases sales contracts must be written.

rw: Negligence is failing to use reasonable care, causing harm to another. The person need not have meant to hurt anyone.

ww.Deliberately harming another person for: Deliberately harming someone for gain is an intentional wrong. Negligence is a failure of care, not intent.
ww.Declining to sign a contract of sale at: Declining to sign a contract is a free choice. It is not negligence.
ww.Following every safety rule perfectly at: Following every safety rule perfectly is the opposite of negligence. It is careful behavior.

rw: Negligence means failing to take reasonable care. Ignoring a spill for an hour is a clear failure that led to injury.

ww.Antitrust law: Antitrust law is about competition and monopolies. A slip on a spill is not a market issue.
ww.Copyright law: Copyright law protects creative works. A spill and an injury have nothing to do with it.
ww.Price fixing: Price fixing is an agreement between rivals on prices. It does not relate to a customer slipping.

rw: A patent gives exclusive rights to an invention for a set time. It stops others from making or selling the invention without permission.

ww.Exclusive rights to a brand name or a lo: Rights to a brand name or logo belong to a trademark. A patent protects inventions.
ww.Exclusive rights to a book or a song for: Rights to a book or song belong to copyright. A patent covers new inventions.
ww.Permission to run a business in the stat: Permission to run a business is a license. A patent protects an invention.

rw: Copyright protects original creative works such as books, music and art. It starts when the work is created and fixed.

ww.Legal protection for brand names and log: Protection for brand names and logos is a trademark. Copyright protects creative works.
ww.Legal protection for inventions made by: Protection for inventions is a patent. Copyright covers creative expression.
ww.Legal protection for company trade secre: Trade secrets are protected by confidentiality law. Copyright covers creative works.

rw: Copyright protects original creative works automatically, as soon as they are written down or recorded. A new song is covered from the moment it is created.

ww.Trademark: A trademark protects brand names and logos. It does not cover a song that has been written.
ww.Trade permit: A trade permit is not a form of protection. It is not a protection for a song.
ww.Patent right: Patent rights protect inventions. A song is a creative work, so copyright applies.

rw: Limited liability means owners are not personally responsible for business debts beyond what they invested. Their personal assets are generally safe.

ww.Owners are exempt from all taxes on any: Limited liability does not exempt owners from taxes. Income is still taxed.
ww.Owners are fully responsible for all bus: This describes unlimited liability, as in a general partnership. Limited liability is the opposite.
ww.Owners cannot lose any of their own mone: Owners can still lose what they invested. Limited liability caps the loss at their investment.

rw: A sole proprietorship is not separate from its owner. The owner is personally responsible for all debts.

ww.A corporation firm: A corporation is a separate legal entity, so owners are not personally liable. It does not give unlimited liability.
ww.A nonprofit corporation: A nonprofit corporation is a separate entity with limited liability. It does not make the owner personally liable.
ww.A limited liability firm: A limited liability company protects its owners from the firm's debts. Unlimited liability is the opposite.

rw: At-will employment means either side may end the job at any time for any lawful reason. Both the employer and employee are free to leave.

ww.Employers must provide a reason for ever: Employers do not have to give a reason in at-will employment. They may end the job for any lawful reason.
ww.Employees can be fired only after a writ: A written warning and hearing are not required in at-will employment. Those are protections found in some contracts.
ww.Employees must give a year's notice befo: Employees do not need to give a year's notice. At-will employees can quit at any time.

map.Hiring only workers with disabilities fo: Paying every worker with a disability twice the normal wage

rw: The ADA requires reasonable accommodations for qualified workers with disabilities. Examples include accessible workspaces or adjusted schedules.

ww.Hiring only workers with disabilities an: The ADA does not require hiring only workers with disabilities. It bans discrimination and requires fair access.
ww.Closing any offices that lack ramps to t: The ADA does not require offices to close for lacking ramps. It requires reasonable accommodations.
ww.Paying every worker with a disability tw: The ADA does not require employers to pay workers with disabilities extra. It requires equal treatment.

rw: Antitrust law promotes competition and prevents unfair monopolies. It aims to protect consumers and smaller businesses.

ww.Require large firms to merge with each o: Antitrust law does not force firms to merge. It aims to keep competition alive.
ww.Set prices for all goods and services so: Antitrust law does not set prices. Markets decide most prices.
ww.Protect monopolies from competitors so f: Antitrust law does the opposite of protecting monopolies. It limits them.

rw: Antitrust law bans price fixing, where rivals secretly agree on prices. Customers are harmed because competition is removed.

ww.Minimum wage law covering hourly pay: Minimum wage law covers hourly pay. Price agreements between rivals fall under antitrust law.
ww.Truth in lending law on loan terms: Truth in lending law covers loan terms. It does not address price agreements between competitors.
ww.Child labor law on young workers: Child labor law limits work by young people. It has nothing to do with price agreements.

rw: A communication barrier is something that blocks a message from being understood. Examples are noise, jargon, language differences and distractions.

ww.A tool that makes messages clearer to th: A tool that makes messages clearer helps communication. A barrier blocks it.
ww.A rule that requires all messages to be: A rule to keep messages short is not a barrier. It may even help clarity.
ww.A meeting held weekly by the staff at th: A weekly meeting is a way to communicate. It is not a barrier.

rw: Feedback is the receiver's response that shows how the message was understood. It lets the sender confirm or fix their message.

ww.The first words a sender says to the rec: The first words a sender says are the opening. Feedback comes from the receiver.
ww.The channel used to send a message, such: The channel is the medium used to send a message. Feedback is the response.
ww.A written copy of the message that is ke: A written copy kept by the sender is a record. Feedback comes back from the receiver.

rw: Active listening means fully focusing on the speaker and responding thoughtfully. It shows respect and helps you understand.

ww.Interrupting to share your own view of t: Interrupting to share your own view is not listening. Active listening focuses on the speaker.
ww.Waiting for your turn to talk to the oth: Waiting for your turn to speak means you are not listening. Active listening engages with what is said.
ww.Looking at your phone while someone talk: Looking at your phone shows no attention. It is the opposite of active listening.

rw: Paraphrasing is restating what you heard to confirm understanding. It is a core part of active listening and shows the customer they were heard.

ww.Changing the subject right away at once: Changing the subject ignores the problem. It does not show listening.
ww.Ignoring the customer and citing policy: Ignoring the customer and citing policy dismisses their concern. It is not listening.
ww.Interrupting to take control of the call: Interrupting takes over the call. It does not confirm understanding.

rw: Nonverbal communication is a message sent through body language, tone and facial expression. It often shows feelings that words do not.

ww.Messages sent through email and text onl: Email and text are written messages. Nonverbal communication does not use words.
ww.Messages sent in spoken words only, with: Spoken words are verbal communication. Nonverbal communication uses gestures, tone and expression.
ww.Messages sent only in writing on a page: Writing is written communication. Nonverbal communication works without words.

rw: Words that say excited but a look at the floor with crossed arms send mixed signals. Audiences tend to believe body language over words.

ww.Strong enthusiasm shown by her own words: Her words show enthusiasm, but her body does not. The audience will notice the mismatch.
ww.No message at all that the audience can: The audience will pick up on her body language. People always read nonverbal cues.
ww.A clear, consistent message because the: Her words and body language do not agree. The message is not clear or consistent.

rw: A company-wide email or announcement reaches everyone at once. It is fast, consistent and can be recorded.

ww.A private talk with each single person: A private talk with each person would take far too long for 200 people. It is also not consistent.
ww.A single phone call to one supervisor: A call to one supervisor reaches only one person. It does not inform 200 staff.
ww.A rumor passed between coworkers: A rumor can be wrong. It is not a reliable way to share a policy change.

rw: An agenda lists the topics to be covered in a meeting. It keeps the meeting focused and on time.

ww.To announce the company's profits for th: Company profits are in financial reports. An agenda is about the meeting.
ww.To record what happened in a past meetin: Recording a past meeting is the job of minutes. An agenda looks ahead.
ww.To list every attendee's job title and p: Job titles and pay are HR information. An agenda does not list them.

rw: Meeting minutes are the official written record of what happened in a meeting. They note decisions and who is to act.

ww.A summary of customer surveys from the y: Customer surveys are summarized in survey reports. Meeting minutes record a meeting.
ww.The length of time a meeting lasts in ho: The time a meeting lasts is its duration. Minutes are a written record.
ww.A list of topics for a future meeting of: A list of future topics is an agenda. Minutes record what has already happened.

rw: Concise writing helps readers understand the message quickly. They can act on it without wading through extra words.

ww.It prevents readers from replying to it: Concise writing does not stop replies. It makes messages easy to answer.
ww.Longer messages are always more polite: Longer messages are not always more polite. They can waste the reader's time.
ww.Short messages always hide the real mean: Short messages do not hide meaning. Being brief means cutting needless words.

rw: A good subject line says what the email is about. 'Meeting moved to Thursday at 2 p.m.' is specific and tells the reader what to expect.

ww.Hello there, a quick note for you: A vague subject like 'Hello there' does not say what the email is about. It may be skipped.
ww.Please read this immediately or else: A threatening subject sounds rude. It creates stress.
ww.Important!!! Read this right now please: Many exclamation marks look unprofessional. Subject lines should be clear and calm.

rw: Being honest, respectful and offering next steps shows care. It helps keep the customer's trust.

ww.Send it late at night without explanatio: Sending bad news late at night with no explanation is thoughtless. It leaves the customer confused.
ww.Wait until the customer asks about it fi: Waiting for the customer to ask delays the news. Customers prefer prompt, direct information.
ww.Hide it inside a long message of details: Hiding news in a long message is evasive. It can mislead.

rw: Jargon is specialized words that outsiders may not understand. It can confuse customers and clients.

ww.A formal business letter sent to a clien: A formal business letter is a document type. Jargon is a type of language.
ww.A clear explanation written in plain wor: A clear explanation in plain words is the opposite of jargon. Jargon uses specialized words.
ww.A greeting used at the start of a call t: A greeting at the start of a call is a courtesy. It is not jargon.

rw: Explaining again in plain language helps the customer understand. It fixes the barrier created by technical terms.

ww.Ignore the confusion and move on: Ignoring the confusion leaves the customer lost. The technician should help them understand.
ww.End the conversation immediately: Ending the conversation leaves the problem unsolved. It would hurt customer relations.
ww.Use even more technical words: More technical words would increase the confusion. The technician should simplify.

rw: Persuasion is influencing others to accept an idea or take action. It uses reasons and evidence, not force.

ww.Ignoring others' opinions on the subject: Ignoring opinions is not persuasion. Persuading means engaging with others.
ww.Forcing others to obey without any choic: Forcing others to obey is coercion. Persuasion lets people choose.
ww.Repeating a statement louder than before: Repeating louder does not persuade. It lacks reasons.

rw: Tone in writing is the writer's attitude shown through word choice. It can be friendly, formal or rude, and shapes how the reader reacts.

ww.The font used in a document, with its co: Font, color and size are formatting. Tone is about attitude.
ww.The length of a message in words and lin: Length is the size of a message. Tone is about attitude.
ww.The loudness of a speaker in a large roo: Loudness belongs to speech. In writing, tone comes through words.

rw: A customer service standard is a set expectation for how customers should be treated. It ensures consistent service.

ww.A price that a customer pays for a good: The price paid is a cost to the customer. A service standard is about treatment.
ww.A discount offered once a year to all of: A yearly discount is a promotion. It is not a service standard.
ww.A product that customers return to the s: A returned product is a return. A standard is a guideline for service.

rw: Apologizing, fixing the problem and offering a small gesture shows care. It repairs the guest's experience.

ww.Ignore the complaint of the guest and do: Ignoring the complaint leaves the guest unhappy. It breaks the hotel's promise a second time.
ww.Blame the guest for arriving much too ea: Blaming the guest is unfair and rude. The hotel made the promise.
ww.Tell the guest the wait was normal for t: Saying the wait was normal contradicts the 5-minute promise. It would anger the guest.

rw: A complaint is a statement that a product or service did not meet expectations. It helps a firm find and fix problems.

ww.A compliment about good service from a b: A compliment is praise. A complaint says something fell short.
ww.An order for more products from a custom: An order for more products is a purchase. It is not a complaint.
ww.A request for a store's hours of busines: A request for store hours is a simple question. It is not a complaint.

rw: Listening without interrupting and offering a solution calms the customer. It shows respect and fixes the problem.

ww.Blame another department for the delay i: Blaming another department shifts responsibility. It does not help the customer.
ww.Tell the customer to calm down and walk: Telling a customer to calm down and walking away dismisses them. It makes them angrier.
ww.Argue to prove that the customer is wron: Arguing to prove the customer wrong damages the relationship. Even when right, it loses goodwill.

rw: Customer retention is keeping existing customers over time. Loyal customers keep buying and often recommend the firm.

ww.Losing customers on purpose each year: Losing customers on purpose is the opposite of retention. Retention keeps them.
ww.Attracting only brand-new customers: Attracting new customers is acquisition. Retention is about keeping current ones.
ww.Selling to customers one time only: Selling only once is a one-time sale. Retention aims for repeat business.

rw: New customers cost more to attract through marketing and discounts. Keeping existing customers is usually cheaper.

ww.Existing customers never need any servic: Existing customers do need service. Retention takes effort.
ww.Retention requires no effort from the fi: Retention requires effort, such as good service. It is not effortless.
ww.New customers always pay higher prices t: New customers do not always pay more. The main reason is acquisition cost.

rw: A customer survey is used to learn customers' opinions and satisfaction. It shows what to improve.

ww.Setting the company's tax rate for the n: Tax rates are set by governments. A survey asks customers questions.
ww.Printing price tags for the store's good: Price tags are printed by the store. A survey is a research tool.
ww.Hiring new employees for the firm each y: Hiring is done through recruitment. Surveys study customers.

rw: A loyalty program rewards customers for repeat purchases. It gives points, discounts or perks to encourage them to come back.

ww.A program that removes all customer feed: It does not remove feedback. Many programs collect feedback.
ww.A program that limits the products custo: It does not limit products. It encourages buying.
ww.A program that charges customers extra f: It rewards customers, so no extra fees are charged for buying.

rw: A free drink after ten purchases rewards repeat visits. The goal is to encourage customers to return.

ww.Stop buying other items: A free drink does not stop customers buying other items. It brings them back.
ww.Raise the price of coffee: A free drink does not raise the price of coffee. It is a reward.
ww.Cut its costs per sale: Giving away drinks does not cut costs. It adds a cost to win loyalty.

rw: Empathy means understanding and acknowledging how the customer feels. It helps staff respond with care.

ww.Rushing the customer to leave the shop a: Rushing a customer to leave shows no care. Empathy means taking time to understand.
ww.Ignoring emotions to focus on rules and: Ignoring emotions to focus on rules is the opposite of empathy. Empathy notices feelings.
ww.Agreeing with every demand a customer ma: Empathy does not mean agreeing with every demand. It means understanding the feelings.

rw: Apologizing, acknowledging the impact on the party and offering to fix it shows empathy. It treats the problem as real.

ww.Delays happen all the time, so it is no: Saying delays are no big deal dismisses the customer's feelings. It shows no empathy.
ww.There is nothing I can do about it for y: Saying there is nothing you can do gives up. It shows no care.
ww.You should have ordered the cake much ea: Blaming the customer is unkind. It avoids responsibility.

rw: A surplus occurs when quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded. Prices tend to fall until the market clears.

ww.When quantity demanded is above the quan: Quantity demanded above supply is a shortage. A surplus is the opposite.
ww.When a firm earns a profit in a year of: Profit is earnings. A market surplus concerns supply and demand.
ww.When supply and demand are equal at some: When supply and demand are equal, the market is at equilibrium. There is no surplus.

rw: A shortage occurs when quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied. Prices tend to rise until demand and supply balance.

ww.When a firm has too many workers on the: Too many workers is overstaffing. A shortage is about goods in a market.
ww.When supply and demand are equal at some: When supply and demand are equal, the market is at equilibrium. There is no shortage.
ww.When quantity supplied is above the quan: Supply above demand is a surplus. A shortage is the opposite.

rw: A console that sells out within minutes at list price means demand exceeds supply at that price. A shortage exists, and prices may rise.

ww.The market is at equilibrium now: At equilibrium supply meets demand, so the console would not sell out in minutes. A sell-out shows demand is higher.
ww.Supply exceeds demand at that price: If supply exceeded demand, the console would stay on shelves. A quick sell-out shows the opposite.
ww.The price is too high for buyers: If the price were too high, buyers would not rush to buy. A sell-out suggests the price is low.

rw: Elasticity of demand shows how much quantity demanded changes when price changes. Elastic demand responds a lot, inelastic demand responds little.

ww.How much a product costs the firm to mak: The cost to make a unit is production cost. Elasticity is about buyers' response to price.
ww.How quickly a product is delivered to th: Delivery speed is a logistics matter. It does not describe elasticity.
ww.How many stores sell the product in the: The number of stores is market coverage. It does not describe elasticity.

rw: Insulin is a necessity with no close substitute for the patient. Demand barely changes when price rises, so it is inelastic.

ww.A specific brand of potato chips: A specific brand of chips has many substitutes. Buyers can switch, so demand is elastic.
ww.A restaurant meal at a nice cafe: A restaurant meal is a choice that people can skip when prices rise. Demand is elastic.
ww.A luxury vacation trip abroad each year: A luxury vacation is a want. Buyers cut back when prices rise, so demand is elastic.

rw: GDP is the total value of goods and services produced in a country. It is the main measure of economic size.

ww.The total money held by the government i: The government's cash is public finance. GDP measures output.
ww.The number of people employed in the nat: The number employed is an employment figure. GDP measures production.
ww.The average price of goods in the shops: Average price of goods is a price index. GDP measures output.

rw: When prices rise faster than pay, purchasing power falls. Prices rose 4 percent and pay only 2, so the worker can buy less.

ww.It rises: Purchasing power rises only if pay grows faster than prices. Here prices outpaced pay.
ww.No change: There is a change. Prices outpaced pay, so the worker's buying power fell.
ww.It doubles: Purchasing power does not double. It fell because pay did not keep up with prices.

rw: Unemployment is being without a job while actively seeking work. It is a key measure of the labor market.

ww.Having a job that you enjoy every day of: Having a job you enjoy is employment. Unemployment is being without work.
ww.Working part-time by choice, with pay an: Part-time work by choice is employment. Unemployment is without a job while seeking one.
ww.Choosing not to work at all, for any rea: Choosing not to work means not being in the labor force. Unemployed people are looking for work.

rw: Fiscal policy is government decisions about taxes and spending. Governments use it to influence the economy.

ww.A bank's lending rules for loans to its: A bank's lending rules are credit policy. Fiscal policy is government action.
ww.Central bank decisions about interest ra: Interest rates are set by the central bank. That is monetary policy.
ww.A company's decisions about the pricing: A company's pricing is business strategy. Fiscal policy is for governments.

rw: Monetary policy is central bank action that influences interest rates and money supply. It aims to control inflation and support growth.

ww.Government decisions about taxes and spe: Taxes and spending are fiscal policy. Monetary policy is run by the central bank.
ww.A store's decisions about the prices of: A store's prices are business decisions. Monetary policy is for the economy.
ww.A firm's decisions about hiring and firi: Hiring and firing is a business matter. Monetary policy concerns money.

rw: Raising interest rates makes borrowing costlier and cools spending. That slows inflation.

ww.Print more money: Printing more money would add to inflation. The Fed would not do this to slow it.
ww.Cut taxes for all: Cutting taxes is fiscal policy and would add spending. It would not slow inflation.
ww.Lower interest rates: Lowering interest rates would boost spending and could raise inflation further.

rw: A trade deficit is when a country imports more than it exports. It means more money flows out for goods than comes in.

ww.When a country stops all of its trade ab: Stopping all trade is a trade ban. A deficit is when imports exceed exports.
ww.When a country exports more than it impo: Exporting more than importing is a trade surplus. A deficit is the reverse.
ww.When a government spends more than it ta: A government spending more than it takes in is a budget deficit. A trade deficit concerns imports and exports.

rw: Exports of $300 billion less imports of $340 billion leaves a deficit of $40 billion. Imports are higher than exports.

ww.A surplus of $40 billion: A surplus would mean exports exceeded imports. Here imports are bigger.
ww.A deficit of $240 billion: $240 billion does not follow from the figures. Subtract exports from imports to get the gap.
ww.A deficit of $640 billion: $640 billion adds the two figures. The balance is their difference, $40 billion.

rw: Self-regulation means managing your emotions and impulses in healthy ways. It helps you stay calm and make good choices.

ww.Acting on every feeling at once, whateve: Acting on every feeling at once is the opposite of self-regulation. It means no control.
ww.Avoiding every stressful task at work al: Avoiding every stressful task is avoidance. Self-regulation means managing stress.
ww.Hiding all emotions from everyone else a: Hiding all emotions is suppression. Self-regulation means handling emotions well.

rw: Self-regulation is controlling emotions and impulses. Pausing before replying calmly after harsh criticism is a clear example.

ww.Self-promotion: Self-promotion is seeking attention. Pausing to answer calmly is about control.
ww.Rivalry for prizes: Rivalry is competing against others. The worker is staying calm.
ww.Procrastination: Procrastination is delaying a task. Pausing before replying is a deliberate choice.

rw: Social awareness is recognizing and understanding other people's emotions. It helps you respond with care and read a room.

ww.Ignoring other people's feelings at work: Ignoring others' feelings is the opposite of social awareness. It means being unaware.
ww.Having many social media followers who w: Social media followers are an audience. Social awareness is about understanding feelings.
ww.Talking louder than others in the room a: Talking louder is not awareness. It ignores others.

rw: Relationship management is building and keeping positive relationships with others. It includes communication, teamwork and resolving conflict.

ww.Keeping score of other people's mistakes: Keeping score of mistakes damages relationships. It is not management.
ww.Avoiding all contact with coworkers at w: Avoiding contact does not build relationships. It cuts them off.
ww.Winning every argument at the office wit: Winning every argument damages trust. Relationship management seeks cooperation.
